UDLCO CRH case report: Recurrent stroke as a result of osmotic demyelination syndrome?

 

Case Report Summary (IMRAD Format)

 

Introduction

 

Central pontine myelinolysis (CPM), a core component of osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS), classically results from rapid fluid/electrolyte correction—chiefly chronic hyponatremia. However, emerging clinical evidence demonstrates that acute, severe shifts in serum osmolality driven by glycemic fluctuations can independently trigger demyelination within the basis pontis. This summary outlines a diagnostic journey where an incidental neuroimaging finding prompted back-tracking history taking, uncovering a complex interplay of drug-induced chronic kidney disease (CKD), glimepiride-induced hypoglycemia, and family-administered free-water hydration that precipitated ODS.

 

Methods

 

A man in his 60s presented to the outpatient department with acute right-sided hemiparesis and ipsilateral upper motor neuron (UMN) facial paralysis of 2 days' duration. Notably, he had a history of a similar hemiparetic episode that had fully resolved. Initial diagnostics included a comprehensive metabolic panel and a brain MRI (T2/FLAIR sequences). Due to an atypical, non-crossed anatomical presentation, a secondary, targeted "back-tracking" interview was conducted with family members to construct a meticulous timeline of the patient's pre-hospital metabolic state.

 

Results

 

Neuroimaging Identification: The brain MRI revealed a well-demarcated, symmetric hyperintensity confined strictly to the ventral pons (basis pontis), sparing the dorsal tegmentum.
Anatomical Correlation: This lesion selectively disrupted un-decussated descending corticospinal tracts and adjacent corticobulbar fibers heading to the contralateral facial nucleus, perfectly explaining the clinical presentation of concurrent right hemiparesis and right UMN facial palsy (sparing the forehead).
Historical Back-Tracking Findings: The secondary anamnesis revealed that the patient had developed CKD secondary to prolonged use of alternative (Ayurvedic) medications for his diabetes and previous stroke. He was recently prescribed glimepiride (a long-acting sulfonylurea). Due to his compromised renal clearance, the glimepiride accumulated, inducing profound, prolonged hypoglycemia. Unaware of the glycemic drop, family members attempted to revive the lethargic patient by administering heavy amounts of plain drinking water without glucose.

 

Discussion

 

In the presence of underlying CKD, glimepiride accumulation precipitated severe neuroglycopenia. The subsequent administrative error of introducing a large free-water load—in an attempt to correct what was mistaken for simple dehydration or fatigue—created an acute, dramatic drop in extracellular tonicity. When euglycemia/osmolality was eventually restored or shifted rapidly during this period, the localized oligodendrocytes within the densely packed, rigid framework of the basis pontis underwent catastrophic osmotic stress and apoptosis, resulting in CPM. This highlights how an initially suspected "recurrent ischemic stroke" was actually an entirely metabolic demyelinating phenomenon.

 

Keywords

 

Central Pontine Myelinolysis (CPM)
Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome (ODS)
Glimepiride-Induced Hypoglycemia
Basis Pontis
Corticobulbar Tract
Alternative Medicine Nephropathy (Ayurvedic)
Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)

 

Thematic Analysis of the Diagnostic Journey

 

+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|               THEMATIC TRACE OF THE CASE                    |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|  [Theme 1: The Neuroanatomical Paradox]                     |
|  - Right body weakness + Same-sided (Right) UMN Face Palsy  |
|  - Spares the Dorsal Tegmentum (Rules out Millard-Gubler)   |
|                             ↓                               |
|  [Theme 2: Neoplastic/Ischemic Mimicry]                     |
|  - Presented like a classic "Recurrent Ischemic Stroke"     |
|  - MRI unexpectedly points to Central Pontine Myelinolysis  |
|                             ↓                               |
|  [Theme 3: Alternative Medicine & Renal Vulnerability]      |
|  - Heavy Ayurvedic use for metabolic comorbidities          |
|  - Induces subclinical CKD, delaying drug clearance         |
|                             ↓                               |
|  [Theme 4: The Hypoglycemic / Hydration Cascade]            |
|  - Glimepiride accumulates -> Severe hypoglycemia          |
|  - Well-meaning family gives free water instead of glucose  |
|  - Triggers the fatal osmotic shifts in the basis pontis    |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
The Neuroanatomical Paradox as a Diagnostic Pivot:

 

The patient presented with an "UMN-on-UMN" pattern affecting the same side (right body and right lower face). This ruled out classic dorsal tegmental brainstem syndromes like Millard-Gubler, which feature crossed deficits (contralateral limb weakness but ipsilateral lower motor neuron facial weakness due to direct facial nerve fascicle involvement). The pure motor tract involvement localized the issue exclusively to the ventral basis pontis, serving as the first true hint toward ODS.

 

Ischemic/Stroke Mimicry vs. Metabolic Reality: The presentation was naturally treated as a recurrent acute ischemic stroke. The incidental detection of CPM on MRI completely altered the diagnostic trajectory, forcing clinicians to shift from a vascular workup to an investigative metabolic audit.

 

The Silent Catalyst (Alternative Medicine-Induced CKD): Chronic use of unmonitored Ayurvedic formulations for his underlying diabetes and prior stroke created an unrecognized state of renal impairment. This subclinical CKD served as the physiological setup, drastically prolonging the half-life of his oral hypoglycemic agent.

 

The Iatrogenic Misstep of Layperson Hydration: The crux of the demyelination was a severe mismatch between clinical reality and home management. Family members misread neuroglycopenic lethargy, treating it with free water rather than simple sugars or a concentrated glucose source. This diluted the extracellular compartment rapidly, driving water into vulnerable pontine astrocytes and oligodendrocytes, paving the way for myelinolysis when systemic shifts corrected.

 

Literature Review: How Common is Non-Hyponatremic/Glycemic ODS?

 

Historically, osmotic demyelination was considered strictly synonymous with the overly aggressive correction of low serum sodium ($>8\text{ to }12\text{ mEq/L per 24 hours}$). However, a growing body of medical literature acknowledges that ODS can be heavily attributed to severe glycemic fluctuations, independently of sodium abnormalities.

 

1. The Prevalence and Recognition of Glycemic ODS

 

While ODS is estimated to occur in roughly $0.06\%$ of generalized hospital admissions, cases presenting purely from glycemic variability (extreme hyperglycemia, Diabetic Ketoacidosis, Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State, or severe hypoglycemia) are rare but steadily increasing in reporting frequency.
Literature reviews indicate that the fundamental driving force is not the sodium ion itself, but the velocity of change in total effective serum osmolality. Glucose is a highly effective osmole; rapid shifts in its concentration cause water to shift across the blood-brain barrier just as violently as sodium deviations do.

 

2. Hypoglycemia and "Glucose Reperfusion" Stress

 

Cases analogous to this patient—where severe hypoglycemia acts as the instigator—have been documented under a specific pathophysiological framework known as glucose reperfusion injury.

 

During prolonged neuroglycopenia, the energy-dependent ion pumps ($Na^+/K^+\text{-ATPase}$) of brain cells begin to fail. This leads to an intracellular accumulation of ions and localized cytotoxic edema.

 

When free water is rapidly introduced, or when glucose is later aggressively resupplied during resuscitation, it causes a sharp spike in extracellular tonicity relative to the damaged cells. Water is forcefully sucked out of the oligodendrocytes, leading to acute cell shrinkage, oxidative stress, blood-brain barrier disruption, and subsequent non-inflammatory demyelination of the basis pontis.

 

3. Vulnerability in Comorbid States (CKD and Malnutrition)

 

Large-scale systematic reviews of atypical ODS highlight that it rarely occurs in a vacuum. It heavily favors patients with underlying metabolic vulnerabilities.
Just as chronic alcoholism and liver disease predispose patients to classic CPM, chronic kidney disease acts as a powerful potentiator for glycemic ODS. CKD not only causes unpredictable pharmacokinetics of medications like glimepiride, but it also alters baseline blood-brain barrier permeability and depletes organic brain osmolytes, making the basis pontis uniquely fragile to even minor osmotic movements.

Please provide a diagrammatic neuroanatomical explanation of the text below:


That's an excellent neuroanatomical question. 👆


The apparent "paradox" you've identified — right hemiparesis with a right UMN facial palsy from a pontine lesion — actually makes perfect anatomical sense when you distinguish **where** in the pons the lesion sits: **ventral (basis pontis) vs. dorsal (tegmentum).**


---


**THE TWO PONTINE SYNDROMES — WHY THEY DIFFER**


**1. Millard-Gubler (Ventral Pontine Tegmentum Lesion) — the "classic" you're taught:**

- Lesion in the **dorsal/tegmental** pons.

- Hits the **corticospinal tract** → contralateral hemiparesis.

- Hits the **exiting facial nerve fascicles** (after they loop around CN VI nucleus, before they exit the pontomedullary junction) → **ipsilateral LMN facial palsy.**

- Offending side: LEFT pons → RIGHT hemiparesis + LEFT LMN facial palsy.


Why LMN? Because the facial nerve fascicles have already left the facial nucleus — you're hitting the peripheral nerve fibers themselves, producing a complete ipsilateral facial droop (forehead included).


---


**2. Basis Pontis Lesion (Pure Motor Tract) — THIS PATIENT'S PATTERN:**

- Lesion confined to the **ventral pons (basis pontis)** — the territory of descending white matter tracts.

- Hits the **corticospinal tract** → contralateral hemiparesis.

- Hits the **corticobulbar fibers** destined for the facial nucleus — these fibers run with the corticospinals and **have not yet decussated** at this level.



- Offending side: LEFT basis pontis → **RIGHT hemiparesis + RIGHT UMN facial palsy.**


Why UMN and ipsilateral to the hemiparesis? Because the corticobulbar fibers to the facial nucleus are still ipsilateral at the pontine level — they haven't crossed yet. A left pontine lesion knocks out the motor commands heading to the right facial nucleus. The facial nucleus itself and its exiting axons (in the tegmentum) are completely spared. The result is a **contralateral UMN-type facial weakness** — sparing the forehead (bilateral UMN innervation to the upper face) but weakening the lower face.


---


**WHY THIS FITS OSMOTIC DEMYELINATION (CPM)**


This is the signature of **Central Pontine Myelinolysis** — osmotic demyelination preferentially affects the **central pons and basis pontis**, where the transverse pontocerebellar fibers and densely packed descending motor tracts create a vulnerable osmotic microenvironment. The tegmentum (housing CN nuclei and exiting fibers) is relatively spared early on. That's exactly why you get a "pure motor tract" syndrome: contralateral hemiparesis + contralateral UMN facial palsy — an UMN-on-UMN pattern with **same-sided deficits**, not crossed.


---


**In summary:** The lesion is in the left basis pontis. Corticospinal + corticobulbar fibers are both still ipsilateral at this level and both go to the contralateral side. Both are hit before decussation. Right-sided UMN hemiparesis + right UMN facial palsy. No LMN component because the tegmentum is spared. That's ODS, not Millard-Gubler.

To map out this clinical picture anatomically, we need to look at a transverse cross-section of the pons and track exactly where the descending motor pathways travel relative to the cranial nerve nuclei.

The diagram below maps the descending pathway of the corticospinal tract through the brainstem. Notice how at the level of the basis pontis, the fibers are bundled tightly together in the ventral portion before they descend to the medulla to undergo decussation (crossing over).

Descending Course of the Corticospinal Tract through the Basis Pontis. Source: VectorMine / Getty Images

The Neuroanatomical Cross-Section: Tegmentum vs. Basis Pontis

Think of a cross-section of the middle-to-lower pons divided into two distinct functional zones by an imaginary horizontal line:

                      [ DORSAL / POSTERIOR ]
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       PONTINE TEGMENTUM                       |
|  * CN VII (Facial) Nucleus      * CN VI (Abducens) Nucleus    |
|  * Exiting CN VII Fascicles     * Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus|
+===============================================================+  <-- Boundary line
|                         BASIS PONTIS                          |
|  * Corticospinal Tracts (descending motor to limbs)           |
|  * Corticobulbar Tracts (descending UMNs to CN nuclei)        |
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
                      [ VENTRAL / ANTERIOR ]

Tracing the Two Distinct Pathologies

By visualizing this cross-section, we can see exactly why the patient's presentation points directly to the basis pontis (as seen in Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome/CPM) rather than the dorsal tegmentum (Millard-Gubler Syndrome).

Scenario A: Millard-Gubler Syndrome (Dorsal Tegmental Lesion)

When a lesion occurs dorsally in the tegmentum, it strikes the structures after the motor commands have already split or processed:

  • CN VII Fascicles: The lower motor neuron (LMN) fibers traveling outward from the facial nucleus are obliterated. Because these fibers supply the ipsilateral side of the face entirely, you see a full ipsilateral LMN facial palsy (inability to smile or wrinkle the forehead on the side of the lesion).

  • Corticospinal Ventral Extension: If the lesion is large enough to extend slightly ventral or involve adjacent tracts, it catches the corticospinal fibers before they cross in the medulla, leading to a contralateral hemiparesis.

  • Result: Alternating/crossed hemiplegia (e.g., Left brainstem lesion = Left face drop + Right body weakness).

Scenario B: Pure Basis Pontis Lesion (The Patient's Pattern)

In Central Pontine Myelinolysis, the demyelination preferentially targets the fat, densely packed tracts running through the ventral basis pontis. The dorsal tegmentum remains completely untouched.

      LEFT BASIS PONTIS LESION                EFFECT ON THE BODY
+----------------------------------+     +--------------------------+
| [Corticospinal Tract]            |     | RIGHT SIDE OF THE BODY   |
| Caught BEFORE medullary          | --->| Hemiparesis/Spasticity   |
| decussation                      |     | (Contralateral)          |
+----------------------------------+     +--------------------------+
| [Corticobulbar Tract]            |     | RIGHT LOWER FACE         |
| Caught BEFORE crossing to the    | --->| UMN Facial Palsy         |
| right CN VII nucleus             |     | (Forehead Spared)        |
+----------------------------------+     +--------------------------+

  1. The Corticobulbar Fiber Trajectory: Upper motor neurons destined for the facial nucleus travel in the corticobulbar tract alongside the corticospinal fibers in the basis pontis. At this horizontal level of the left pons, the fibers meant for the right facial nucleus have not yet crossed the midline.


  1. The Impact: A lesion in the left basis pontis interrupts these descending left UMN fibers. The right facial nucleus in the right tegmentum loses its main upstream drive.

  2. Forehead Sparing: Because the upper face portion of the right facial nucleus receives bilateral UMN input (from both the left and right hemispheres), the intact right hemisphere keeps the forehead moving normally. The lower face, relying strictly on the now-disrupted contralateral (left) tract, droops.

  3. Result: A clean contralateral UMN facial palsy that mirrors the contralateral hemiparesis perfectly on the right side of the body.

Share a diagrammatic neuroanatomical image for how the dorsal tegmental lesion of millard gubler syndrome as described above 


This image effectively maps the anatomical reason for the classic "crossed" or alternating paralysis presentation—where a brainstem lesion affects cranial nerves on the same side and long tract motor function on the opposite side.
